rows.title: Color
rows.text: You very likely have two kinds of color-sensing cell, where humans have three. The Eurasian red squirrel, the California ground squirrel and the thirteen-lined ground squirrel all have two kinds, and in each of them the large majority of cones are one kind, with only a few of the other. If you are an eastern gray squirrel or a fox squirrel, your two kinds sense best in blue and in green.
rows.note: Left out nanometer figures and any claim about which colors look alike, since no record states what dichromacy looks like for squirrels.

rows.title: Speed
rows.text: A lamp that flashes 60 times a second looks steady to a human, and nobody has measured where flicker starts to look steady to you if you are a gray squirrel or a fox squirrel. The squirrels that have been measured differ a lot: a golden-mantled ground squirrel sees flicker above 100 flashes a second, an American red squirrel about 60, and a southern flying squirrel only 10 to 15.
rows.note: Left out the chipmunk and California ground squirrel figures to keep the row short; the two golden-mantled records (120 and 108) are given as "above 100".

rows.title: Field of view and sharpness
rows.text: If you are an eastern gray squirrel, you can resolve stripes up to about 4 cycles a degree, and if you are a fox squirrel, about 2, where a human reads about 30. In the Eurasian red squirrel the cone cells are packed most densely in a horizontal streak with no sharp spot, and you very likely have the same if you belong to its genus, Sciurus, like the gray and fox squirrels. Nobody has measured how wide your field of view is or how much of it both eyes share.
rows.note: Left out the chipmunk and ground squirrel streak/best-vision figures since they cover other genera; the 3.9 figure comes from one gray squirrel.
